claimed.text: Tal Levesque, who wrote as Jason Bishop III, told Adam Gorightly by email in November 2015 that Castello was a creation, a myth, and that he built the two original Dulce articles from the account of a heavily medicated woman he names as Ann West, mixed with his own research. He had maintained for years before that Castello was real.

In the same message Levesque described making 100 large packets of material on underground bases, genetic research and hidden science and sending them to authors and lecturers, who mixed it into their talks, articles and books. The confession reached the board through Gorightly's 2021 book as reproduced by Hayakawa.

Every specific number in the modern claim comes from Schneider's lecture at Post Falls, Idaho on 8 May 1995: he said he helped build an addition to the base, that it goes down seven levels and over 2.5 miles deep, and that in a 1979 firefight he shot two aliens and about seventy people were killed.

Bennewitz summarised his own investigation in a report of late 1981 titled Project Beta; he is the first person to attach a facility claim to Dulce, and he connected Hansen's 1980 account to it after he had begun to suspect a site there.

Doty has said publicly that as an AFOSI agent he supplied Bennewitz with false documents and information as part of an official effort; Greg Bishop says he was told that the Air Force flew Bennewitz to Archuleta Mesa and showed him a site dressed with props to draw his attention away from Kirtland.

Lear heard of Dulce from a woman named Ann West and developed his hypothesis in 1988; on the board's reading, this is the same name Levesque gives, so two entry points into the literature appear to run back through one person.
Cooper says his knowledge came from TOP SECRET/MAJIC material he read in 1970-1973 on a Pacific Fleet intelligence briefing team; his own statement is the only source for that access.

contested.text: Hayakawa, who has worked the Dulce question since 1988 and favours investigating it, concludes that the facility does not seem to exist; Greenewald found no evidence that Castello ever existed; and a sceptic's review of satellite imagery of the mesa found nothing there.

The case against has its own limits: the confession was read only as reproduced from Gorightly's book, the imagery review cites a single blog post, and Hayakawa's report that a retired colonel denied Castello was ever employed rests on an anonymous source.

On the board's reading, no employment of Schneider by anyone was ever documented; the firm, Corps of Engineers and Navy attributions rest on a memorial biography and his own lectures. His casualty figure also differs within the one source, about seventy in his words and sixty-six in its introduction.

Doty, asked by George Knapp on camera, called the story that he brainwashed or harmed Bennewitz false in every aspect and said Bennewitz did this to himself, while giving Bennewitz's recorded signals an extraterrestrial meaning; on the board's reading, his statements, including his denials, establish only what he said.
Bishop, author of the standard account, limits what he says was done to Bennewitz to Moore being told to hand him the Aquarius document, and calls Bennewitz his own worst enemy.

Gabe Valdez, the only official investigator in the story, is cited in the Dulce literature as a supporting voice, but the opened report carries no statement from him that a base exists; the book from his files ties the animal deaths to contamination testing after Gasbuggy.

On the board's reading, the Castello name carries no jurisdiction, employer or dates in any version, so no records search can even be formulated; and Gasbuggy's adjacency to the mesa does not show that it caused the rumour.

lead.text: Dulce Base is the allegation of a joint human and alien facility under Archuleta Mesa, New Mexico. No record the board has opened places any facility there, a researcher who has worked the question since 1988 concludes it does not seem to exist, and the story's central insider, Thomas Castello, was confessed in 2015 as an invention by the man who says he wrote the original articles and mailed a hundred packets to make the story look independently sourced.

record.text: The Department of Energy's record of Project Gasbuggy: on 10 December 1967 the Atomic Energy Commission detonated a 29-kiloton device at 4,227 feet, twelve miles southwest of Dulce, to stimulate natural gas production; it was the Plowshare Program's first gas stimulation experiment, and the gas produced in 1968-1969 kept measurable radioactive constituents.

The AEC decommissioned the site in 1978, injecting liquid radioactive waste into the former cavity; soil sampling followed over the next decades, and surface remediation removing 5,562 cubic yards of contaminated soil was completed in 2004. The DOE Office of Legacy Management holds long-term stewardship of the 640-acre site.

Cooper's The Secret Government, dated 23 May 1989 and first delivered at the MUFON symposium that July, contains the word Dulce zero times in forty-nine pages; it places alien bases under Indian reservations in the Four Corners area, and grades itself as a hypothesis resting partly on sources he cannot divulge or vouch for.

The photograph of bodies in a chamber circulated for years as Castello's leaked proof is a frame from the 2000 film The 6th Day, as John Greenewald showed in 2016; the identification can be checked by anyone against the film.

The AFOSI record from Kirtland in 1980, carrying the name of Special Agent Richard Doty, documents security police sightings over the Manzano area and that Bennewitz's reporting was under official notice.
The only documented part of Schneider's family story is his father, a US Navy captain buried at Willamette National Cemetery; Bennewitz's burial record shows a Second World War Coast Guard seaman.

summary.text: The rumour grew in stages: Paul Bennewitz from about 1979, then Myrna Hansen's 1980 account, Tom Adams's cattle-mutilation work in the early 1980s, John Lear in 1988, and Phil Schneider only in 1995, according to Norio Hayakawa's dated chronology.

The real ground is Dulce and, twelve miles away and just west of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation, the site of Project Gasbuggy, a 1967 federal nuclear detonation now under the Department of Energy's stewardship; the board records adjacency and precedence, not that Gasbuggy caused the rumour.
On the board's reading, Dulce is its own worked example of manufactured corroboration: the many later sources that agree about Dulce agree because they were supplied from one origin by one method.
The frame of alien bases under Four Corners reservations reached a mass audience through Bill Cooper's 1989 paper, which does not contain the word Dulce at all.
